screens.title: Every story has a skeleton
lines: You've devoured enough books to FEEL the moment a story 'gets good' — that feeling has a map.
Today we x-ray stories: the mountain every plot climbs, the trouble that powers it, and the message hiding inside the bones.

vocab.meaning: the chain of events in a story — what happens, in order
the struggle that powers a story: a character pushing against some opposing force
the message about life a story shows, stated as a complete idea — not just one word

sequences.title: Reading Quests: Clues + What You Know

screens.title: You already read minds (sort of)
lines: When your cat sits glaring beside an empty bowl, nobody has to TELL you dinner is late — you read the clues.
Authors play the same game: they plant clues and trust you, the detective, to crack them. That detective move is called an inference.

vocab.meaning: a conclusion you reach by combining clues from the text with what you already know
the exact words or details in the text that back up an idea
what a passage is mostly about — the point all the other details support

items.prompt: Let's x-ray a story you've known forever — the Tortoise and the Hare — and map it onto the plot mountain.

steps.text: Every story climbs a PLOT MOUNTAIN with five stops. Stop one, the EXPOSITION: we meet the racers and their world — the hare is fast and boastful, the tortoise slow and steady. No trouble yet, just the setup.
RISING ACTION: the race begins and tension builds. The hare sprints ahead, gets cocky, and settles in for a nap under a tree — while the tortoise keeps plodding, step after step.

check.question: Which event belongs to the rising action?
options: The hare naps while the tortoise keeps walking — trouble is building
We learn that the hare is fast and boastful
The crowd goes home after the race

steps.text: CLIMAX — the peak of the mountain, the moment of highest tension: the hare jolts awake and sees the tortoise only steps from the finish line. Everything hangs on this one desperate sprint.
Then the mountain slopes down. FALLING ACTION: the hare's dash falls just short. RESOLUTION: the tortoise crosses the line, and the story settles into its ending — steady effort beat careless speed.

check.question: What makes the climax the climax?
options: It's the peak of tension, where the outcome gets decided
It's the longest part of the story
It's wherever the main character is introduced

steps.text: Five stops, one mountain: exposition → rising action → climax → falling action → resolution. You can map ANY story onto it — even a three-second cat video has a tiny mountain. 🐱

items.prompt: Your turn to x-ray one. Mini-story: Pip the kitten lives in a cozy bakery. One morning the flour bin tips over and buries the day's recipe cards. Pip digs and sneezes and digs — and the oven timer rings with NOTHING ready to bake. At last she paws the final recipe card free; the baker bakes, the shelves fill, and Pip earns the first warm roll.

lines: We meet Pip in her bakery world, before any trouble → that's the [[exposition]]
The timer rings with nothing ready — the peak of tension → the [[climax]]
The shelves fill and Pip gets her warm roll — the story settles → the [[resolution]]

items.hint: Setup at the base, peak of tension at the top, settled ending at the far side.
items.explanation: Setup → exposition, highest tension → climax, settled ending → resolution. You just x-rayed a whole story.

items.prompt: Last x-ray tool: TOPIC vs THEME. A topic names a subject; a theme is what the story SAYS about it. Finish the labels for the Tortoise and the Hare.

lines: 'Racing' and 'pride' each name a subject in a single word — each one is a [[topic]]
'Steady effort beats careless speed' states the story's full message — that is the [[theme]]
A theme is always a complete [[idea|sentence|thought]], never just one word

items.hint: One of them fits on a sticky note; the other needs a whole sentence.
items.explanation: Topics are one-word subjects; themes are full ideas a story argues about life.

items.prompt: On the plot mountain, which part introduces the characters and setting BEFORE the trouble starts?
options: Exposition
Climax
Falling action
Resolution
items.hint: It's the base camp of the mountain — where you meet everyone.
items.explanation: The exposition is the setup: characters and setting first, trouble later.

items.prompt: Climb the plot mountain: put the five stages in story order.

sequence: Exposition
Rising action
Climax
Falling action
Resolution

items.hint: Up the mountain to the peak of tension, then down the other side.
items.explanation: Stories climb: setup, building trouble, peak, unwinding, settled ending.

items.prompt: 'The new ball of yarn was as round as a little moon.' Which device is this?
options: Simile
Metaphor
Personification
Hyperbole
items.hint: Hunt for the comparison words 'as … as'.
items.explanation: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as' — here, 'as round as a little moon'.

items.prompt: Match each device to its example line.

pairs: The frosting was as smooth as glass
The bakery was a furnace by noon
The kettle grumbled on the stove
Six sleepy cats sat on the sunny step

items.hint: Simile uses 'as'; metaphor says IS; personification gives human moods; alliteration repeats a starting sound.
items.explanation: Each device has a fingerprint: 'as', is, human behavior, repeated sounds.

items.prompt: Rosa and her sister both want the last ball of gray yarn, and neither will give in. Which conflict is this?
options: Character vs character
Character vs self
Character vs nature
Character vs society
items.hint: Who — or what — is Rosa pushing against?
items.explanation: Two people pushing against each other is character vs character.

items.prompt: These five events make one tiny storm story. Put them in the order the plot mountain would climb them.

sequence: A storm warning crackles over the lighthouse radio
Wind rips the signal flag from the tower
Minka the cat drags the flag back up the spiral stairs
The rescued flag waves the fishing boats safely home
Minka sleeps by the stove, a small unnoticed hero

items.hint: Follow cause and effect: warning, disaster, brave deed, rescue, rest.
items.explanation: Each event causes the next — that chain of cause and effect IS the plot.

items.prompt: Sort each mini-scenario by the type of conflict driving it.

Character vs character: Two bakers feud over a stolen secret recipe
A knight duels the bandit king at the bridge
Character vs nature: A shepherd is trapped on a cliff ledge by a blizzard
A sailor rows against a rising storm
Character vs self: A singer battles her own stage fright
A boy fights the urge to peek at his sister's diary

items.hint: Ask: is the hero pushing against a person, the wild world, or something inside themselves?
items.explanation: Name the opposing force and the conflict names itself: another person, nature, or a feeling within.

items.prompt: 'I pressed my nose to the bakery window and decided the éclairs were definitely calling my name.' Which point of view?
options: First person
Third person limited
Third person omniscient
Second person
items.hint: Who is telling this — and what tiny word gives it away?
items.explanation: The narrator says 'I' and 'my' — a character inside the story is speaking, so it's first person.

items.prompt: 'Fog curled through the empty street, and somewhere behind her, a gate creaked twice.' What MOOD do these lines create for the reader?
options: Eerie
Cheerful
Triumphant
Cozy
items.hint: Mood is the feeling that settles over YOU as you read.
items.explanation: Fog, emptiness, and an unseen creaking gate build an eerie, uneasy feeling — that's mood, the reader's side of the page.

items.prompt: Name each device. (You've seen both on the x-ray table already.)

lines: 'The storm rattled the windows and muttered all night' treats the storm like a person — that's [[personification]]
'I have knitted this row a million times' exaggerates wildly — that's [[hyperbole]]

items.hint: One device gives human behavior to a thing; the other stretches the truth past breaking.
items.explanation: Storms can't mutter (personification), and nobody knits a million rows (hyperbole).

items.prompt: 'By July, Aunt Bea's kitchen is a furnace.' Which device is this?
options: Metaphor
Simile
Personification
Alliteration
items.hint: No 'like', no 'as' — the sentence says the kitchen IS something.
items.explanation: A metaphor declares one thing IS another: kitchen = furnace, no comparison words needed.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about THEME are true. Find the lie.

truths: A theme is a message about life, stated as a complete idea
One story can carry more than one theme
data.lie: A theme is a single word, like 'jealousy'

items.hint: One of these is actually describing a topic.
items.explanation: A single word like 'jealousy' is a TOPIC. The theme is what the story says ABOUT jealousy, in a full idea.

items.prompt: 'Mara hoped the snow would cancel school. Across town, her teacher wished for exactly the same thing, though neither would ever admit it.' Which point of view?
options: Third person omniscient
Third person limited
First person
Second person
items.hint: Count how many characters' private thoughts the narrator can enter.
items.explanation: The narrator dips into TWO minds — Mara's and the teacher's — so it's the all-knowing third person omniscient.

items.prompt: A bard wrote four lines about night. Exactly one is NOT a metaphor — tap it.

segments: Her braid was a rope of midnight.
The moon was a silver coin spent on the sea.
The dark was as thick as new wool.
Sleep was a tide that pulled her under.

items.hint: Metaphors say one thing IS another. One line compares a different way.
items.explanation: 'As thick as new wool' uses 'as … as', so it's a simile. The other three each declare one thing IS another.

items.prompt: 'Jonas counted his coins for the third time and slid them across the counter. The shopkeeper's face gave away nothing — Jonas had no idea if it would be enough.' Which point of view?
options: Third person limited
Third person omniscient
First person
Second person
items.hint: The narrator says 'he' — but whose head are we locked inside?
items.explanation: We hear Jonas's thoughts but are locked out of the shopkeeper's — third person limited rides along with one mind only.

items.prompt:
A sparrow mocked the old cat for dozing all day, calling her lazy while he showed off loops in the air. When a hawk dove at the yard that afternoon, the show-off froze — and the 'lazy' cat exploded off her windowsill, scattering feathers until the hawk gave up. The sparrow never trusted appearances again.

What is the THEME of this fable?
items.answer: Appearances can hide what someone is truly capable of
options: Appearances can hide what someone is truly capable of
Cats and birds
Hawks always lose in the end
Sleeping all day makes you stronger
items.hint: Which choice is a complete message about life — and matches what the sparrow learned?
items.explanation: 'Cats and birds' is just a topic, and the others miss the point: the 'lazy' cat's hidden strength is the lesson.

items.prompt: Sort each original line by its figurative device.

Simile: Her purr was like a tiny engine
The dough rose slowly, like a sleepy moon
Metaphor: The library was a forest of stories
His temper was a kettle near the boil
Personification: The last cookie begged to be eaten
The old stairs complained under our feet

items.hint: 'Like' flags one family; IS flags another; human behavior in objects flags the third.
items.explanation: Similes compare with 'like', metaphors declare IS, and personification lets cookies beg and stairs complain.

items.prompt: 'Of course our hero the rooster, brave defender of the barnyard, had bravely hidden behind the smallest hen.' What is the author's TONE toward the rooster?
options: Mocking
Admiring
Fearful
Neutral
items.hint: Do the praise words match what the rooster actually did?
items.explanation: Calling a hider 'brave' twice is sarcasm — the author is mocking the rooster, and tone is the author's attitude.

items.prompt: A storm scene leaves YOU shivery and tense, while the author describes the storm in delighted, playful words. Which one is the TONE?
items.answer: Delighted and playful — the author's attitude
options: Delighted and playful — the author's attitude
Shivery and tense — the reader's feeling
The storm itself
The nighttime setting
items.hint: Tone belongs to the writer; mood belongs to the reader.
items.explanation: Tone = the author's attitude (playful delight here); the shivery feeling you get is the mood.

items.prompt: Read the mini-scene, then finish the story x-ray. 'Captain Idra stood at the rail as the first hailstones hit. For three days the sea had pushed her ship backward, and her crew's eyes had begun to ask the question no one would say aloud.'

lines: The captain's struggle against the sea is a character vs [[nature]] conflict
The unspoken question builds tension, so this scene belongs to the [[rising action|rising]]

items.hint: Name the opposing force first; then ask where on the mountain tension is still BUILDING.
items.explanation: The sea is a force of nature, and mounting dread before the peak is rising action.

items.prompt:
Nadia had practiced her solo for months, and tonight the concert hall glowed. Halfway through the first verse, a string on her guitar snapped with a crack that echoed to the back row. The audience held its breath while Nadia stared at the broken string, fingers frozen. Then, with the whole hall silent, Nadia made her choice: she shifted her grip and played on. Afterward, her teacher called it the bravest music he had ever heard.

Which sentence is the CLIMAX — the peak where the outcome is decided?
items.answer: Then, with the whole hall silent, Nadia made her choice: she shifted her grip and played on.
options: Nadia had practiced her solo for months, and tonight the concert hall glowed.
Halfway through the first verse, a string on her guitar snapped with a crack that echoed to the back row.
The audience held its breath while Nadia stared at the broken string, fingers frozen.
Then, with the whole hall silent, Nadia made her choice: she shifted her grip and played on.
Afterward, her teacher called it the bravest music he had ever heard.
items.hint: Tension RISES while things go wrong — the climax is where the character's choice settles it.
items.explanation: The snap and the frozen fingers build tension; the moment Nadia chooses to play on decides everything. That decision is the peak.

items.prompt: The myth of Persephone, x-rayed. Match each plot stage to its event.

pairs: Persephone gathers flowers in a sunlit meadow
Hades takes her below while Demeter's grief lets the crops fail
Zeus demands her return — but she has eaten six pomegranate seeds
The gods strike a deal: part of each year below, part above
Every spring the world blooms when she rejoins her mother

items.hint: Find the single moment the whole outcome hinges on — that's your climax; everything after it unwinds.
items.explanation: The pomegranate seeds are the hinge of the whole myth; the deal and the seasons flow downhill from that moment.

items.prompt:
All summer, Jo and Wren built a raft together. The day it finally floated, they argued so fiercely about its name that Wren stomped home. The raft sat untouched for a week — until Wren returned with a paintbrush and painted JO'S FOLLY on the bow, and Jo laughed until she cried. They shoved off together, captains of a boat with a ridiculous name neither would change.

Which statement BEST expresses the theme?
options: Real friendship can survive disagreement
Friendship
Never argue with a friend or you will lose them forever
Building a raft takes all summer
items.hint: One option is only a topic, and one is contradicted by the ending. Which message does the story actually prove?
items.explanation: 'Friendship' is just the topic, and the friends DON'T lose each other — the story shows their bond outlasting the fight.

items.prompt: A theatre goblin labeled the plot stages of Pip the bakery kitten's tale. Tap the label that is WRONG.

segments: Exposition: We meet Pip the kitten in her cozy bakery home.
Rising action: The flour bin tips and buries the day's recipe cards.
Resolution: The oven timer rings with NOTHING ready to bake.
Falling action: The baker bakes the rescued recipe and the shelves slowly fill.

items.hint: A resolution SETTLES a story. Does that moment feel settled to you?
items.explanation: The timer ringing over an empty oven is the peak of tension — the CLIMAX, not a resolution. Resolutions calm the story down.

items.prompt:
The day after the championship, Priya's medal hung on her bedpost, where it caught the morning light. She had imagined this exact sunbeam all season. Yet at breakfast she found herself talking not about the final point, but about the bus rides, the inside jokes, the way the whole team groaned in harmony whenever Coach announced wind sprints. The medal was gold. The groaning, she decided, had been golden.

Which statement BEST expresses the theme?
items.answer: The shared journey can matter more than the prize at the end
options: The shared journey can matter more than the prize at the end
Winning medals
Hard work always ends in a gold medal
Trophies should be displayed where the light catches them
items.hint: Reread the last two sentences — which 'gold' does Priya value more?
items.explanation: Priya calls the team's groaning 'golden,' quietly ranking the journey above the medal. That contrast carries the theme.

items.prompt: Read this tiny scene like a detective: 'Amal opened the front door. Her cat shot past her, fur soaked flat, and refused to come out from under the bed all evening. Outside, the gutters were still dripping.'

steps.text: A detective reads a room; a reader reads a page. Step one: collect the CLUES the text actually gives. Clue one: the cat's fur is soaked flat. Clue two: the gutters are still dripping.
Step two: add what YOU already know about the world — dripping gutters mean recent rain, and no cat soaks itself on purpose.

check.question: Which of these is a CLUE from the text, not outside knowledge?
options: The gutters are still dripping
Rain falls from clouds
Most cats dislike water

steps.text: Step three: combine them. Clues + what you know = the cat got caught outside in a rainstorm. Notice: the text never SAYS it rained. You concluded it — that's an INFERENCE.
That's the detective's move you'll use on every Reading Quest: text clues + what you know = inference. Some call it reading between the lines.

check.question: What makes 'it rained' an inference rather than a stated fact?
options: The passage never says it — we concluded it from clues
The narrator announces the weather report
It's a wild guess with no support

items.prompt: Finish this inference like a detective. The scene: 'Omar slid his pie onto the contest table, then checked the clock for the third time and re-tied his apron twice.'

lines: Clue from the text: Omar keeps checking the clock and fidgeting with his apron
What I know: people fidget and clock-watch when they feel [[nervous|anxious|worried]]
Inference: Omar is anxious about how the pie contest will go

items.hint: When have YOU re-tied, re-checked, re-counted something? What were you feeling?
items.explanation: Fidgeting plus clock-watching are classic clues — your own experience fills in the feeling: nervous.

items.prompt: One more — this time pair the inference WITH its evidence. The scene: 'Every evening at five, long before any human reached for the can opener, Biscuit was already seated beside her bowl, eyes fixed on the cupboard.'

lines: Inference: Biscuit has learned the family's feeding [[routine|schedule]]
Evidence: she is waiting by her bowl at [[five|5]], before anyone even moves toward the food

items.hint: The evidence is the exact detail in the text that would convince a doubter.
items.explanation: An inference is only as strong as its evidence — and a cat seated at five o'clock sharp is strong evidence indeed.

items.prompt:
SPROCKET OF THE CINNAMON WHEEL

Sprocket the cat had worked at the Cinnamon Wheel Bakery for three years, though no one had ever hired him. He arrived each morning at six, just as Mr. Abel unlocked the door, and took up his post on the wide windowsill — the one spot where sunlight, oven warmth, and the smell of rising dough met in the air like three friends shaking hands.

Customers thought Sprocket was decoration. The regulars knew better. When the line grew long and toddlers began to wail, Sprocket would stroll the counter's edge, tail high, until the crying turned to giggling. When old Mrs. Okafor came in on Thursdays, he sat beside her chair while she drank her tea, because Thursdays were the days she visited the bench where her husband used to feed pigeons.

Mr. Abel never said any of this out loud. He simply set out a saucer of cream each evening, marked the calendar every Thursday with a small paw print, and left the windowsill cushion exactly where it was, even when the new shelves arrived and every other corner of the bakery changed.

What is this story MOSTLY about?
items.answer: A bakery cat who quietly looks after the people around him
options: A bakery cat who quietly looks after the people around him
Step-by-step instructions for baking bread
A baker who wants to get rid of a stray cat
A woman who opens her own bakery
items.hint: Main idea = the point that EVERY paragraph helps build.
items.explanation: Every detail — calming toddlers, sitting with Mrs. Okafor, the saucer of cream — builds one idea: Sprocket quietly takes care of people.

Why does Mr. Abel mark every Thursday with a paw print?
items.answer: He treats Sprocket's Thursday visits with Mrs. Okafor like a real appointment
options: He treats Sprocket's Thursday visits with Mrs. Okafor like a real appointment
He is reminding himself to give Sprocket a bath
He stamps every page of the calendar for decoration
Thursday is the day the new shelves arrive
items.hint: What happens at the bakery every Thursday — and who notices?
items.explanation: Mrs. Okafor's hard Thursdays are when Sprocket sits with her; the paw print shows Mr. Abel treats that comfort like real work.

In the first paragraph, Sprocket 'took up his post on the wide windowsill.' Here, 'post' means…
items.answer: his regular spot, like a guard's assigned place
options: his regular spot, like a guard's assigned place
a wooden fence pole
a letter dropped in the mail
an online message
items.hint: Swap each meaning into the sentence — only one makes sense for a cat reporting to work.
items.explanation: Sprocket 'works' at the bakery, so his post is his duty station — context picks the meaning.

Two of these statements about the story are true. Find the LIE.

truths: Sprocket arrives at the bakery at six each morning
Mr. Abel keeps the windowsill cushion in place even after the bakery gets new shelves
data.lie: Mr. Abel often tells customers how helpful Sprocket is

items.hint: Check the last paragraph carefully — what does Mr. Abel do instead of talking?
items.explanation: The story says Mr. Abel 'never said any of this out loud' — he shows his thanks with cream and paw prints, not words.

items.prompt:
THE WEAVER AND THE NORTH WIND

Long ago, in a village pinned between the mountains and the sea, the North Wind grew jealous of human warmth. Each winter he howled down the slopes, snuffing out fires and scattering roofs like playing cards. The villagers begged the goddess of the hearth for help. But it was Melia, a weaver with calloused fingers and a patient eye, who answered.

'Great Boreas,' she called from the cliff, 'I will weave you a cloak worthy of a king of storms — if you can tear it, our village is yours. If you cannot, you will only ever visit us gently.' The wind, who was as vain as he was loud, roared his agreement.

For thirty nights Melia wove. She did not choose wool. She spun thread from things no wind has ever beaten: the roots of mountain pines, the patience of stones, the last warmth of a banked fire. When Boreas wrapped the cloak around his shoulders, he swelled himself into a hurricane and blew — and the cloak only settled closer, snug as snow on a sleeping field.

Three times he raged. Three times the weave held. At last the North Wind sighed, and his sigh was almost gentle. From that day on, winter in the village arrived like a guest, not a thief.

Why does Melia's plan work on Boreas?
items.answer: She counts on his vanity — he cannot resist a challenge that flatters his power
options: She counts on his vanity — he cannot resist a challenge that flatters his power
She knows he is secretly afraid of the goddess of the hearth
She uses magic that controls the weather
He is too tired from the long winter to argue with her
items.hint: Reread how the wind is described right before he agrees to the bargain.
items.explanation: The text calls him 'as vain as he was loud' — Melia baits that vanity with 'a cloak worthy of a king of storms,' and he can't refuse.

The wind is described as 'as vain as he was loud.' In this myth, 'vain' means…
options: overly proud of himself
useless and hopeless
impossible to see
freezing cold
items.hint: What kind of personality falls for flattery about being 'a king of storms'?
items.explanation: Boreas accepts because the wager flatters him — vanity here is excessive pride, not the 'in vain' kind of useless.

items.prompt:
THE WEAVER AND THE NORTH WIND

Long ago, in a village pinned between the mountains and the sea, the North Wind grew jealous of human warmth. Each winter he howled down the slopes, snuffing out fires and scattering roofs like playing cards. The villagers begged the goddess of the hearth for help. But it was Melia, a weaver with calloused fingers and a patient eye, who answered.

'Great Boreas,' she called from the cliff, 'I will weave you a cloak worthy of a king of storms — if you can tear it, our village is yours. If you cannot, you will only ever visit us gently.' The wind, who was as vain as he was loud, roared his agreement.

For thirty nights Melia wove. She did not choose wool. She spun thread from things no wind has ever beaten: the roots of mountain pines, the patience of stones, the last warmth of a banked fire. When Boreas wrapped the cloak around his shoulders, he swelled himself into a hurricane and blew — and the cloak only settled closer, snug as snow on a sleeping field.

Three times he raged. Three times the weave held. At last the North Wind sighed, and his sigh was almost gentle. From that day on, winter in the village arrived like a guest, not a thief.

Which sentence BEST states a theme of this myth?
items.answer: Patience and cleverness can succeed where raw force fails
options: Patience and cleverness can succeed where raw force fails
Weaving and winter
The strongest one always wins in the end
Never make a bargain with a stranger
items.hint: Toss out the topic and anything the ending contradicts.
items.explanation: 'Weaving and winter' is a topic, and the strongest one LOSES here — the myth shows patient craft outlasting a hurricane.

THE PROP ROOM (a scene from a play)

SETTING: The school prop room, ten minutes before the talent show. Shelves of painted swords and paper crowns. JUNE, eleven, paces in a costume cape, mouthing words silently. Her brother TEO, nine, watches from an overturned bucket.

TEO: You've practiced that speech a hundred times.
JUNE (still pacing): A hundred and six.
TEO: So you know it.
JUNE: Knowing it isn't the problem. (She peeks through the curtain at the audience, then snaps it shut.) There are so many of them.
TEO (hopping off the bucket): Want to hear a secret? (He holds out a paper crown.) Last year, before my magic act, my hands were shaking so hard I dropped my cards. Twice.

JUNE (taking the crown slowly, almost smiling): One face.
TEO: One face.

ANNOUNCER (offstage): Next up — June Ramos!
JUNE (whispering, to TEO): Watch me the whole time.

What do the stage directions reveal about June that her spoken lines alone do not fully show?

She has never actually practiced her speech
She is angry that Teo followed her backstage
She plans to skip her performance and go home
items.hint: Read only the words in parentheses and italics — what is June's body doing?
items.explanation: Stage directions are the playwright's camera: pacing, mouthing words, and snapping the curtain shut act out a nervousness June never names.

items.prompt:
from THE LIGHT ON GULL ISLAND — Chapter One

The ferry to Gull Island ran twice a week, and it carried three kinds of passengers: birdwatchers, lighthouse tourists, and people with something to avoid on the mainland. Nora Quinn, age twelve, suspected she was the third kind, even though it was her mother who had packed the suitcases.

'Six months,' her mother had said. 'Just until Grandpa's hip heals. You'll love the lighthouse.'

The lighthouse, Nora learned that first evening, had not been lit in forty years. Ships used satellites now. The great lamp room at the top of the spiral stairs was kept locked, and the key — according to Grandpa — had gone to the bottom of the harbor with a rowboat called the Petrel before Nora was born. He said it cheerfully, the way he said most things, but Nora noticed he told the story while polishing a small brass key he wore on a cord around his neck.

That night, wind moaned around the cottage and Nora couldn't sleep. She counted gulls instead of sheep. She was somewhere past ninety when her dark bedroom suddenly wasn't dark. A slow beam of light swept across her wall — once, then again.

Three stories above her, behind a locked door, the lamp of Gull Island was burning.

Put these events in the order they happened.

sequence: Nora's mother announces a six-month stay with Grandpa
Nora rides the ferry to Gull Island
Grandpa tells the lost-key story while polishing a brass key
Unable to sleep, Nora counts gulls in the dark
A beam of light sweeps across Nora's bedroom wall

items.hint: Careful — the chapter MENTIONS the mother's promise after the ferry, but when did she say it?
items.explanation: Story order isn't always telling order: the mother's 'six months' came before the ferry ride, even though the narrator reports it second.

items.prompt:
ANANSI AND THE POT OF WISDOM (a tale from the Ashanti tradition, retold)

Long ago, Anansi the spider decided that wisdom was far too valuable to leave lying around in everyone's heads. So he crept from village to village with a clay pot, and into it he gathered every scrap of wisdom he could find: the farmer's knowledge of rain, the fisher's knowledge of tides, the grandmother's knowledge of which silences mean sorrow and which mean peace.

When the pot was full, Anansi decided to hide it at the top of the tallest palm tree, where no one else could ever reach it. He tied the pot to his belly and began to climb. But the pot was wide and his legs were thin; with the pot in front of him, his knees scraped and slipped, and for every step up he slid two steps down.

From the foot of the tree, his youngest son watched. 'Father,' the boy finally called, 'wouldn't it be easier to tie the pot to your back?'

Anansi stopped. He had collected all the wisdom in the world — and a child had just handed him a piece he didn't have. He laughed so hard that the pot shook loose, fell, and cracked open, and the wisdom blew away on the wind, a little of it landing on everyone.

Put the events of the tale in order.

sequence: Anansi gathers wisdom from every village into a clay pot
He ties the pot to his belly and starts to climb the palm tree
His son suggests tying the pot to his back instead
Anansi laughs until the pot falls and cracks open
The wisdom scatters on the wind, landing on everyone

items.hint: Follow the pot: filled, carried, questioned, dropped, scattered.
items.explanation: The pot's journey IS the plot — each event pushes the next one over like dominoes.

items.prompt:
THE INVISIBLE ZOO IN THE JAR

A jar of sourdough starter looks like a science experiment napping on the kitchen counter — and that is exactly what it is. A starter begins as nothing but flour and water. Within days, it becomes home to a busy, invisible zoo.

Wild yeast — a microscopic fungus that drifts in flour, in the air, even on your hands — moves into the mixture and begins to eat the sugars in the flour. As the yeast feeds, it releases carbon dioxide, the same gas you breathe out. The gas forms bubbles, which is why a healthy starter looks foamy and rises in its jar as if it were breathing.

The yeast has roommates: bacteria called lactobacilli. They feed alongside the yeast and produce acids, and those acids give sourdough bread its famous tang. The acids also act as bodyguards, making the starter too sour for most harmful microbes to survive.

Bakers 'feed' a starter every day by stirring in fresh flour and water. Skip the feedings and the colony weakens; keep them up and a starter can outlive its baker. Some bakeries in San Francisco still use starters begun more than a century ago — billions of great-great-grandchildren of the original yeast, still making bubbles, still raising bread.

Use the passage to finish the explanation.

lines: As wild yeast eats the flour's sugars, it releases [[carbon dioxide|carbon-dioxide|CO2|co2]] — the gas whose bubbles make the starter [[rise|rises|foam]] in its jar.

items.hint: Both answers hide in the second paragraph.
items.explanation: Yeast eats sugars and breathes out carbon dioxide; the trapped bubbles puff the starter up — and later, the bread.
